questions.explanation: `auto [a, b] = p;` declares a hidden variable `auto e = p;`, which is a copy, and `a` names `e.first`, so the write does not reach `p`. With `auto&`, the hidden variable is a reference to `p`, so `c` names `p.first` and the second write is visible. The first option assumes bindings always alias the initializer, which is only true when the hidden variable is a reference.

options: Well-formed: structured bindings always extend the lifetime of the initializer
Well-formed, but `a` and `b` dangle after the declaration
Ill-formed: the hidden variable is a non-const lvalue reference initialized from a prvalue
Ill-formed: structured bindings cannot have a reference qualifier
questions.explanation: The declaration introduces `auto& e = make();`, and a non-const lvalue reference cannot bind to a prvalue, so the program is ill-formed. Lifetime extension would apply if the binding were allowed, which is why `const auto&` and `auto&&` work. Reference qualifiers on structured bindings are perfectly legal.

options: Well-formed: only public members are bound, so `a` is `y`
Ill-formed, but only because `P` is not an aggregate
Well-formed: structured bindings ignore access control
questions.explanation: With no `std::tuple_size` specialization, the names bind to all non-static data members of `P` in declaration order, and every one of them must be accessible at the point of the declaration. `x` is private and `main` is not a friend, so the program is ill-formed. Private members are not skipped, and aggregate status is irrelevant: binding to members does not use aggregate initialization.

`std::pair` uses the tuple protocol, and `decltype` of an unparenthesized structured binding is its referenced type, `std::tuple_element<0, std::pair<int, int>>::type`, which is `int`. The `&` makes the hidden variable a reference, but it does not change the referenced type. `int&` is what `decltype((a))` gives, because the parenthesized form uses the rule for lvalue expressions.

options: Nothing: ill-formed, because `std::tie` returns a prvalue
Nothing: undefined behavior, because the tuple is a destroyed temporary
questions.explanation: `std::tie(x, y)` returns `std::tuple<int&, int&>`, and `auto` makes the hidden variable a tuple of that type. It holds references to `x` and `y`, so `std::tuple_element<0, E>::type` is `int&` and `a` refers to `x` itself. `auto` produces a new tuple, not new ints, and since the hidden variable is an object rather than a reference to the temporary, nothing dangles.

options: `~Noisy`, `body`, `after`: the temporary dies at the end of the declaration
Undefined behavior: `n` and `i` refer into a destroyed temporary
questions.explanation: The hidden variable is `const auto& e = make();`, a reference bound directly to the prvalue, so the temporary pair has its lifetime extended to that of `e`, the end of the inner block. `body` is printed while the pair is alive, then `~Noisy` at the closing brace, then `after`. The first and last options assume the bindings themselves would need to extend the lifetime; they do not, because `e` already does.

questions.prompt: Both a member `get` and a free `get` exist. What does this program print?
options: Ill-formed: the call to `get` is ambiguous
`3 4` only: `Pt` is an aggregate, so its data members are bound directly
questions.explanation: Because `std::tuple_size<geo::Pt>` is complete, the tuple protocol is used, not direct member binding. [dcl.struct.bind] then uses `e.get<i>()` whenever member lookup for `get` finds a function template whose first template parameter is a non-type parameter, and only otherwise falls back to `get<i>(e)` found by argument-dependent lookup. The two are never put into one overload set, so there is no ambiguity, and the member is called once per binding.

questions.prompt: In C++23, which of these structured binding declarations at block scope is well-formed?
questions.explanation: C++20 allowed the storage class specifiers `static` and `thread_local` on structured binding declarations, alongside `auto` and cv-qualifiers. `constexpr` was not permitted until C++26 (P2686); GCC accepts it in C++23 mode only as an extension with a warning, and Clang rejects it. `inline` and `extern` are not allowed in any version.
